author: Akien (the ruling and the worked inference) + CC (the capture)
text: SYSTEM METRICS SHOULD ALSO BE LEARNING. Akien, verbatim: 'system metrics should also be learning. we wanna watch what it costs to spin up another x, and in future be able to yeah/nay based on data, not a number out of akien's head. but even so, inference can be made: if no x running and 20% cpu, and 1 x = 30%, then we can say, from data, that we prolly don't wanna go over 6 x. keeping an eye on it as we go of course.' THE METHOD, abstracted: measure the BASELINE (the box with none of this thing running), measure the MARGINAL COST of one more, divide the headroom by the margin, and the ceiling falls out. Every term is observable; none is a number a person has to hold. WHAT IT RETIRES: harbor_master's HARBOR_LINES, both values — cpu 75.0 (derived from Akien's measured 6-of-8 crawl point) and memory 1024 (a labelled hypothesis). It also retires an assumption hiding inside the 75, that one builder costs one runnable; his example implies ~2.4 runnable per builder on 8 cores. Nobody has measured it. THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE THING: the 6/8 number was a LEARNED VALUE ALL ALONG — learned from experience, held in Akien's head, and written down nowhere in either repo before 2026-08-04. This is not new learning being invented; it is an existing learned value moving out of a human's head into data the system holds. And 'keeping an eye on it as we go' is the standing half: a marginal cost is not a constant either (it moves with whatever else lives on the host), so the ceiling is a live derivation, not a one-time calibration. ONE THING THE NEW METRIC MADE SAYABLE: 20% + 6x30% = 200% is a coherent statement about a box only because runnable-over-cores has no 100% ceiling (runnable can exceed cores) — roughly 2 runnable per core, about where a box stops being useful. A percentage-of-capacity metric could not have expressed the inference at all; the sampler swapped to runnable on 2026-08-04, one day before the ruling that needs it.
